title: Fire, Grief and Priestly Rules
overview: Just as the priests begin their work, two of Aaron's sons die for offering incense in a way God had not commanded, and the chapter follows with rules for how priests must act near God's presence.

parts.label: A fatal act of worship (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu burned incense in a way the LORD had not commanded, and fire from God's presence struck them dead. The text never says exactly what they did wrong, and Moses only explains that those who serve closest to God must treat him as holy; Aaron, their father, stays silent.

parts.label: No mourning for the priests (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp, still in their priestly tunics, because the dead could not stay near the sanctuary. Aaron and his two remaining sons, freshly anointed for service, are told not to show the usual signs of grief (loose hair, torn clothes) or leave their post, while the rest of Israel may mourn.

parts.label: Clear heads for priests (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: God tells Aaron that priests must not drink alcohol before serving, so they can tell the holy from the ordinary and the clean from the unclean (fit or unfit for worship) and teach the people. Because this rule comes right after the deaths, some have guessed the brothers were drunk, but the text does not say so.

parts.label: The priests' share of food (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Moses reminds the grieving priests which parts of the offerings are theirs. Some grain is so sacred it must be eaten beside the altar, while the breast and thigh lifted up before God may be shared with their families in any ritually clean place.

parts.label: Aaron's answer to Moses (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: Moses is angry that the goat offered for the people's wrongs was burned instead of eaten by the priests, since eating it was part of the ritual. Aaron answers that after losing his sons that day, eating it would not have pleased God, and Moses accepts this, though readers differ on whether Aaron was strictly right.

disagreement: Christians differ on what exactly Nadab and Abihu did wrong, some seeing the problem as worship done their own way rather than God's, and others reading in pride, carelessness or drunkenness that the text does not state.
think: This chapter sets strict rules beside a grieving father whose exception is accepted; where do you think rules should bend for grief, and where should they hold?
